content.title: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives
content.overview: This lesson covers the process of finding the slope of a tangent line to a polar curve r(θ) in the Cartesian xy-plane. By treating the polar equation as a set of parametric equations where θ is the parameter, we can determine the rate of change of y with respect to x.
learning_objectives: Convert polar equations to parametric form using x = r cosθ and y = r sinθ.
Apply the product rule to find the derivatives dx/dθ and dy/dθ.
Calculate the slope dy/dx of a polar curve at a specific value of θ.
Identify the conditions for horizontal and vertical tangent lines on a polar curve.

sections.title: The Parametric Connection
sections.content: To find the slope dy/dx of a polar curve r = f(θ), we must relate the polar variables to the Cartesian plane. We define the coordinates as functions of θ: x(θ) = r(θ)cosθ and y(θ) = r(θ)sinθ. Because r is itself a function of θ, finding the derivatives of x and y requires the product rule. Specifically, dx/dθ = r'(θ)cosθ - r(θ)sinθ and dy/dθ = r'(θ)sinθ + r(θ)cosθ.

sections.title: Calculating the Slope dy/dx
sections.content:
The slope of the tangent line in the xy-plane is the ratio of the rates of change: dy/dx = (dy/dθ) / (dx/dθ). This formula is valid only when dx/dθ is not equal to zero. If dy/dθ = 0 and dx/dθ is non-zero, the curve has a horizontal tangent. If dx/dθ = 0 and dy/dθ is non-zero, the curve has a vertical tangent. If both are zero, the slope is indeterminate and requires further investigation, such as using L'Hôpital's Rule or analyzing the limit.

![A sequence of steps to find the slope of a polar curve: 1. Define x and y in terms of theta. 2. Find r prime of theta. 3. Compute dx/dtheta and dy/dtheta using product rule. 4. Calculate the ratio dy/dx.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/4eb2b2e5-e57f-4a3a-bb37-0cded9c69f66-1786519392944-997.webp)

worked_examples.question: Find the slope dy/dx and the equation of the tangent line for the polar curve r(θ) = 1 + 2sinθ at θ = π/6.
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Evaluate r and r' at θ = π/6. r(π/6) = 1 + 2sin(π/6) = 1 + 2(1/2) = 2. Since r'(θ) = 2cosθ, r'(π/6) = 2cos(π/6) = 2(√3/2) = √3.
Step 2: Find the Cartesian point (x, y). x = r cosθ = 2 cos(π/6) = 2(√3/2) = √3. y = r sinθ = 2 sin(π/6) = 2(1/2) = 1. The point is (√3, 1).
Step 3: Calculate dx/dθ and dy/dθ. dx/dθ = r'cosθ - r sinθ = (√3)(√3/2) - (2)(1/2) = 3/2 - 1 = 1/2. dy/dθ = r'sinθ + r cosθ = (√3)(1/2) + (2)(√3/2) = √3/2 + √3 = 3√3/2.
Step 4: Compute dy/dx. dy/dx = (3√3/2) / (1/2) = 3√3.
Step 5: Write the tangent line equation. Using point-slope form: y - 1 = 3√3(x - √3).

common_mistakes: Assuming the slope dy/dx is simply r'(θ).
Confusing the slope of the tangent line (dy/dx) with the slope of the polar ray (tanθ).
Forgetting to use the product rule when differentiating x = r cosθ and y = r sinθ.
Neglecting to check if dx/dθ is zero before concluding the value of the slope.
exam_tips: Always write out the product rule formulas for dx/dθ and dy/dθ before plugging in values to avoid sign errors.
If asked for a tangent line, remember you need the Cartesian coordinates (x, y), not just the polar coordinates (r, θ).
Double-check your unit circle values; a small error in sin(π/6) or cos(π/6) will invalidate the entire slope calculation.
content.recap: To find the slope of a polar curve, convert to parametric form x = r cosθ and y = r sinθ, use the product rule to find dx/dθ and dy/dθ, and calculate their ratio. The resulting dy/dx represents the slope in the Cartesian plane.

knowledge_claims.content: The Cartesian x-coordinate of a polar point is defined as x = r(θ)cosθ.
The Cartesian y-coordinate of a polar point is defined as y = r(θ)sinθ.
To find dy/dx for a polar curve, calculate the ratio (dy/dθ) divided by (dx/dθ).
The derivative dx/dθ is calculated using the product rule as r'(θ)cosθ - r(θ)sinθ.
The derivative dy/dθ is calculated using the product rule as r'(θ)sinθ + r(θ)cosθ.
A horizontal tangent line occurs on a polar curve when dy/dθ = 0, provided dx/dθ is not zero.
A vertical tangent line occurs on a polar curve when dx/dθ = 0, provided dy/dθ is not zero.
It is a mistake to assume dy/dx is equal to r'(θ) or tan(θ).
Before concluding a slope is finite, one must verify that dx/dθ is not equal to zero at the given θ.
The equation of a tangent line to a polar curve at a point requires the Cartesian coordinates (r cosθ, r sinθ) and the slope dy/dx.
The derivative dy/dx represents the instantaneous rate of change of the y-coordinate with respect to the x-coordinate in the xy-plane.
If both dy/dθ and dx/dθ are zero at a point, the slope dy/dx must be found by taking the limit as θ approaches that value.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Polar Coordinates and Derivatives — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.
options.B: Ratio and Root Tests: Ratio and root limits below one imply absolute convergence and above one imply divergence, while a limit of one is inconclusive.
options.C: Derivative as a Limit: The derivative is the limit of average rates of change and represents instantaneous rate of change or tangent-line slope.
options.D: Exponential, Logarithmic, and Inverse Trigonometric Derivatives: Standard derivatives for exponential, logarithmic, and inverse trigonometric functions combine with product, quotient, and chain rules.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Polar Coordinates and Derivatives — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Taylor and Maclaurin Series: Taylor coefficients are derivatives evaluated at the center divided by factorials, and Maclaurin series are centered at zero.
options.B: Polar Coordinates and Derivatives: Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta.
options.C: Differentiability and Continuity: Differentiability implies continuity, but corners, cusps, vertical tangents, discontinuities, and unequal one-sided derivatives can prevent differentiability.
options.D: Interpreting Derivatives in Context: A contextual derivative must identify the rate, input, units, and meaning at the specified instant rather than report only a number.

items.explanation: Choice B is best because Polar points use radius and angle, and polar slope follows from parametric differentiation of x=r cos theta and y=r sin theta. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.
